title: Encoding and decoding
objectives: Build an encoder and decoder from a list of merges, and measure bytes per token.

screens.title: New text, old merges
screens.prose: The last lesson's toy tokeniser learned four merges from `bid bids bidder bidding`: `bi`, `bid`, ` bid` and ` bidd`. Now it meets new text, `bidding bids`.

state.caption: bidding bids: 12 bytes; the box is a space.

screens.question: Apply the four merges. How many tokens is `bidding bids`?

hints.text: Apply `bi` first, everywhere, then `bid`, then ` bid`, then ` bidd`.
`bidding` starts the text, so no space comes before it.
`bid`, `d`, `i`, `n`, `g`, ` bid`, `s`: 7 tokens.

feedback.correct: Seven: `bid d i n g` then ` bid s`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply each merge in turn and count what is left.

byKey.bytes: That is the byte count, before any merge.
byKey.bidd: You merged `bidd` at the start, but the learned token is ` bidd`, with a space. `bidding` here has no space before it.

explain.text: `bi` and `bid` apply to both words, and ` bid` to the second. ` bidd` needs a space before `bid d`, which the first word lacks, so 7 tokens.

screens.title: Replaying the merges
screens.prose: Encoding replays the merges in the order they were learned, each one everywhere it applies. Step through the four merges on `bidding bids`.
screens.question: Which merge changes nothing here?

options.why: Slide to merge 1: the row drops from 12 to 10 cells.
Slide to merge 2: the row drops from 10 to 8.
Slide to merge 3: the space joins `bid` in the second word.

hints.text: Watch the cell count at each step.
Compare steps 3 and 4.

feedback.correct: ` bidd` finds no space before `bid d`, so it changes nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the step where the cell count stays the same.

explain.text: The ` bidd` merge needs ` bid` followed by `d`. Here `bid d` starts the text with no space, so the merge never fires and we end with 7 tokens.

screens.title: Decoding
screens.prose: Each new id stands for the bytes of its two parts. So every token's bytes can be built up in merge order. **Decoding** joins the bytes of the tokens and reads them as UTF-8.

state.caption: The toy tokeniser's merges, in training order; 98 is b, 105 i, 100 d, 32 a space.

screens.question: How many bytes does token 259 stand for?

hints.text: 259 is 258 followed by 100.
258 is a space followed by 257, which is `bid`.
` bid` is 4 bytes and `d` is 1: 5 bytes.

feedback.correct: Five bytes: a space, b, i, d, d.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Expand 259 into its parts, then those into theirs.

byKey.pair: 259 is made of two ids, but 258 itself stands for 4 bytes.
byKey.no-space: You dropped the space. 258 is space plus `bid`.

explain.text: 259 is 258 plus `d`, 258 is a space plus 257, and 257 is `bid`. So 259 is ` bidd`, 5 bytes.

screens.title: Text it never saw
screens.prose: The toy tokeniser was trained on four English words. Feed it `€5`.

state.caption: The toy tokeniser's merges, in training order; 98 is b, 105 i, 100 d, 32 a space.

screens.question: How many tokens does `€5` become?

hints.text: No merge involves the bytes of `€`.
So every byte stays a token of its own.
`€` is 3 bytes and `5` is 1: 4 tokens.

feedback.correct: Four tokens: `e2`, `82`, `ac` and `35`, the raw bytes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. With no merge to apply, how many tokens is each byte?

byKey.chars: Characters are not tokens here. The euro sign is 3 bytes, and no merge joins them.
byKey.unknown: There is no unknown token: bytes are the fallback, so `€` is spelt out byte by byte.

explain.text: No merge touches these bytes, so each is its own token: 4 tokens, `[226, 130, 172, 53]`. Unseen text still encodes, just less compactly, and decodes back exactly.

screens.title: Compression on held-out text
screens.prose: 200 merges were learned on the first 20,000 characters of the Shakespeare slice. Encode the slice's last 25,000 characters, which the tokeniser never saw.
screens.question: What is the bytes per token on the held-out text? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Divide bytes by tokens.

feedback.correct: $25000 / 13809 \approx 1.8104$, below the 2.0121 on the training text.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the held-out bytes by the held-out tokens.

byKey.inverted: You divided tokens by bytes. Put bytes on top.
byKey.train: That is the training text's figure. Work it out for the held-out row.

explain.text: Held out, each token covers 1.8104 bytes against 2.0121 on the training text. A tokeniser compresses its own training text best. Measure bytes per token on the text you score.

screens.title: Which order?
screens.prose: A tokeniser learned three merges, in this order: `er` as 256, `th` as 257, then `the` as 258 (257 followed by `e`). Encode `the there`; `th` and `he` are its most frequent pairs, twice each.
screens.question: How is the word `there` split?

options.why: You merged `th` first because it is the most frequent pair in this text. Encoding replays merges in training order, and `er` was learned first.
There is no `re` merge. Only learned merges can apply.
No merge makes `there`. Tokens come only from the three learned merges.

hints.text: Apply merge 1 first, everywhere.
After `er` is merged, `there` reads `t h er e`.
Then `th` gives `th er e`, and `the` cannot apply: `th` is followed by `er`, not `e`.

feedback.correct: Training order gives `th er e`, while `the` alone becomes one token.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the merges in the order they were learned.

byKey.freq: That is the frequency-first mistake: it merges by counts in the new text. The same word would then be split one way here and another way in training.

explain.text: Applying `er` first leaves `th er e` for `there`, and `the` merges only in the first word. Replaying in training order makes every text split as the model saw it in training.

screens.title: Losses per token and per byte
screens.prose: Level 2 of `info` measured loss in nats and bits. A loss of $L$ nats per token, with $b$ bytes per token, is $L / b$ nats per byte. Dividing by $\ln 2$ gives bits per byte.

state.caption: Both models scored on the held-out 25,000 characters.

screens.question: The token model scores 4.20 nats per token on the held-out 25,000 characters, where its tokeniser gives 1.8104 bytes per token. What is that in bits per byte? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: First turn nats per token into nats per byte.
$4.20 / 1.8104$ nats per byte.
$4.20 / (1.8104 \times \ln 2) \approx 3.3470$ bits per byte.

feedback.correct: $4.20 / (1.8104 \ln 2) \approx 3.3470$ bits per byte: better than the bigram's 3.5424 on the same text.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the bytes per token, then by $\ln 2$.

byKey.no-ln2: That is nats per byte. Divide by $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$ to get bits.
byKey.per-token-bits: That is bits per token. Spread it over the 1.8104 bytes each token covers.
byKey.times: You multiplied by the bytes per token. A token covers several bytes, so the loss per byte is smaller: divide.

explain.text: Per byte, the token model loses $4.20 / 1.8104$ nats, which is about 3.3470 bits. Its per-token loss looked worse than 2.4554, but both are held out, and per byte it beats the bigram's 3.5424.

screens.title: One unit for every tokeniser
screens.prose:
Bits per byte is a loss that does not depend on the tokeniser:
$$\text{bits per byte} = \frac{L}{b \ln 2}$$
with $L$ the loss in nats per token and $b$ the bytes per token, both on the same text. Bytes per token is the compression ratio.
screens.question: Why is the division by $\ln 2$ there?

options.why: Dividing by $b$ does that. $\ln 2$ changes the unit of information.

options.text: It averages over the two halves of a pair
options.why: Nothing is averaged. One bit is $\ln 2$ nats, so nats divided by $\ln 2$ are bits.

options.text: It corrects for the bigram baseline
options.why: No baseline enters the formula; it is a change of units.

hints.text: How many nats is one bit?

feedback.correct: One bit is $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$ nats, so dividing by $\ln 2$ converts nats to bits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about the units of $L$.

explain.text: $L / b$ is nats per byte, and one bit is $\ln 2$ nats. Two models scored on the same text can then be compared, whatever their tokenisers.

screens.title: Write the encoder and decoder
screens.prose: Write `encode(text, merges)`, returning the list of ids, and `decode(ids, merges)`, returning the string. `merges` is the list from `train_bpe`. Decode with `errors='replace'` so a cut-off character shows as U+FFFD.

state.caption: The toy tokeniser's merges, in training order; 98 is b, 105 i, 100 d, 32 a space.

screens.question: Write `encode` and `decode`.

tests.setup: text = open('tiny-shakespeare.txt').read(); m = train_bpe(text[:5000], 30); s = text[-3000:]

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: the toy merges (`TOY` is defined for you), an unseen euro sign, empty input and merges that must replay in training order. Others try round trips with £ and an emoji, a cut-off character, and 3,000 Shakespeare characters through 30 merges learned from the first 5,000. `merge` and `train_bpe` are defined for you.

mutants.symptom: Applies merges by their frequency in the new text, not in training order.
Decodes without errors='replace', so a cut-off character raises.

hints.text: `encode`: start from the UTF-8 bytes and apply each merge in order with `merge(ids, pair, 256 + k)`.
`decode`: build a dict from id to bytes, starting with `bytes([i])` for the 256 bytes.
Id `256 + k` maps to the bytes of its two parts joined; join the tokens' bytes and call `.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')`.

feedback.correct: Every planted string survives the round trip, and the merges replay in training order.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 needs training order: apply merge 0 first, then 1, then 2, whatever the counts in the new text.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 decodes a cut-off euro sign. Use `errors='replace'`, so it becomes U+FFFD instead of raising.

explain.text: Encoding replays the merge list in order; decoding expands each id to its bytes. Because bytes are the fallback, `decode(encode(s)) == s` for every string.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, each accepted within a relative 1e-8. They are the bigram's 2.4554 nats per character, the worked example, the uniform loss $\ln 65$, one nat on a byte, a loss of 0 and two vendors' figures.

mutants.symptom: Multiplies by the bytes per token instead of dividing.

hints.text: Divide the loss by the bytes per token.
Then divide by `math.log(2)`.
`return loss_nats_per_token / (bytes_per_token * math.log(2))`.

feedback.correct: Your conversion matches on every test.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is the uniform loss $\ln 65$ on one byte per character, which is $\log_2 65 \approx 6.0224$ bits. Check the $\ln 2$.

explain.text: One line: nats per token over bytes per token is nats per byte, and over $\ln 2$ it is bits per byte. The uniform model over 65 characters gives $\log_2 65 \approx 6.0224$.

screens.title: Two vendors, two tokenisers
screens.prose: Two vendors score their models on the same set of research notes. A reports 3.10 nats per token with 3.8 bytes per token. B reports 2.60 nats per token with 3.0 bytes per token.
screens.question: Which model predicts the notes better?

options.text: A: 1.18 bits per byte against B's 1.25
B: 2.60 nats per token is lower than 3.10
options.why: You compared per-token losses across two tokenisers. A's tokens are longer, so each carries more text; convert to bits per byte first.

options.text: Neither: different tokenisers cannot be compared
options.why: They can, once both are put in bits per byte on the same text.

options.text: B: 1.25 bits per byte against A's 1.18
options.why: You read the comparison the wrong way round. Lower loss is better.

hints.text: Convert each to bits per byte.
A is about 1.18 and B about 1.25 bits per byte.

feedback.correct: A wins at about 1.18 bits per byte, though its per-token loss is higher.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put both losses in bits per byte before comparing.

byKey.b: Per-token losses depend on token length. A's tokens cover 3.8 bytes, B's 3.0, so compare per byte.

explain.text: A: $3.10 / (3.8 \ln 2) \approx 1.18$; B: $2.60 / (3.0 \ln 2) \approx 1.25$ bits per byte. A predicts the notes better: the lower per-token loss came from shorter tokens.

ideas: Encoding replays the merges in training order, each everywhere it applies; decoding joins each token's bytes and reads UTF-8.
Bytes are the fallback, so any string encodes and `decode(encode(s)) == s`; unseen text just compresses less.
Bytes per token is the compression ratio; compare models across tokenisers in bits per byte, $L / (b \ln 2)$, on the same text.

formula.name: Bits per byte
formula.note: $L$ nats per token, $b$ bytes per token, on one text.

summary.trap: Applying merges by their frequency in the new text instead of training order, or comparing per-token losses across tokenisers.

quiz.prose: With the toy merges (256 `bi`, 257 `bid`, 258 ` bid`, 259 ` bidd`), a model outputs the ids `[257, 115, 259, 101, 114]`.
quiz.question: What text do they decode to?

options.why: Token 259 starts with a space, so a space separates the words.
259 is ` bidd`, with two d's.
Decoding joins the bytes; the token boundaries leave no spaces.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Expand each id into its bytes and join them.

explain.text: 257 is `bid`, 115 is `s`, 259 is ` bidd`, then `e` and `r`. Joined, that is `bids bidder`.

quiz.prose: A character-level model reads plain English text, one byte per character. Its validation loss is 1.30 nats per character.
quiz.question: What is that in bits per byte? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. With one byte per token, only the unit changes.

byKey.times: You multiplied by $\ln 2$. Bits are smaller units than nats, so the number grows: divide.

explain.text: With $b = 1$, bits per byte is $L / \ln 2$, and $1.30 / \ln 2 \approx 1.8755$.

quiz.question: Why does `decode(encode(s)) == s` hold for every string `s` with a byte-level BPE tokeniser?

options.text: Merges only group bytes; decoding ungroups them
Every string was seen in training
options.why: Most strings were not. Unseen text falls back to bytes, which still decode exactly.

options.text: Each string has one most frequent pair
options.why: Frequency is not used at encoding time; the merge list is replayed as learned.
A full encoding never cuts a character, so nothing needs repairing.

feedback.correct: Grouping and expanding are inverse, so the bytes, and the text, come back unchanged.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does a merge do to the bytes themselves?

explain.text: A merge never changes or drops a byte; it only groups two ids. Decoding undoes every grouping, so the original UTF-8 bytes return.

quiz.prose: A team retrains its tokeniser with more merges. On the same validation text, the loss rises from 2.9 to 3.4 nats per token. Bytes per token rises from 3.1 to 3.9.
quiz.question: Did the model get worse at predicting the text?

options.text: No: bits per byte fell from about 1.35 to about 1.26
Yes: the loss rose from 2.9 to 3.4
options.why: You compared per-token losses across two tokenisers. Longer tokens carry more text each.

options.text: It cannot be told without the old model
options.why: Both figures are on the same text, so bits per byte answers it.

options.text: Yes: bits per byte rose from about 1.26 to about 1.35
options.why: You swapped the two models' figures. Recompute each with its own bytes per token.

feedback.correct: Per byte the loss fell, so the model predicts the text better.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Convert both losses to bits per byte.

explain.text: Before: $2.9 / (3.1 \ln 2) \approx 1.35$. After: $3.4 / (3.9 \ln 2) \approx 1.26$ bits per byte, lower, so better.
